triage.name: Chlamydia Infections
triage.reason: Common STI often asymptomatic or with urethritis/cervicitis; diagnosis reachable by sexual history, exam and NAAT testing.

demographics: Highest rates in sexually active adolescents and young adults, especially women aged 15–24
Rates are higher in non-Hispanic Black and American Indian/Alaska Native populations in the US, largely reflecting differences in access to care and screening rather than behavior
Men who have sex with men have higher rates of rectal and pharyngeal infection

risk_factors.text: Age 25 or younger and sexually active
New sex partner or more than one partner in the past year
Partner with a known STI or partner with symptoms of urethritis
History of a prior chlamydial or other STI
Exchange of sex for money or drugs
Incarceration or recent release from a detention facility

social_history: May be in a new relationship or a relationship they believe is monogamous
May have limited access to routine preventive care
exposures: Unprotected vaginal, anal, or oral sex with an infected partner
Sexual contact with a partner who has urethral discharge or dysuria
Passage through an infected birth canal (neonates)

chief_complaints.text: I don't really have any symptoms — my partner told me they tested positive
I've had some discharge down there that isn't normal for me
My lower belly has been hurting
There's been some bleeding after sex
My testicle hurts and feels swollen

hpi.onset: Gradual; symptoms, when present, usually begin 1–3 weeks after exposure, but many patients never notice a clear onset
hpi.duration: Days to weeks; often present for weeks before the patient seeks care, and frequently detected only on routine screening
hpi.progression: Most infections stay asymptomatic or produce mild symptoms that wax and wane; untreated infection can ascend over weeks to months and cause pelvic inflammatory disease in women or epididymitis in men
hpi.location: Urethra, cervix, rectum, or pharynx depending on exposure; pelvic or lower abdominal pain if infection ascends
hpi.radiation: Pelvic pain may radiate to the lower back or thighs; testicular pain may radiate along the spermatic cord
hpi.quality: Burning or stinging with urination; thin discharge; dull pelvic or scrotal ache
hpi.severity: Usually mild; pelvic inflammatory disease and epididymitis are more painful and can be moderate to severe
hpi.timing: Dysuria is constant with urination; discharge may be noticed most in the morning; pelvic pain is often constant or worse with movement and intercourse
aggravating: Walking or jarring movements (with pelvic involvement)

associated_symptoms.text: Vaginal bleeding between periods or after sex
Rectal pain, discharge, or bleeding with rectal infection

pertinent_negatives: Marked fever and rigors at first presentation
Severe unilateral testicular pain of sudden onset with nausea and vomiting
Missed period with one-sided pelvic pain and vaginal bleeding
Joint swelling and rash preceding the genital symptoms

negatives: Sores on the palms or soles

atypical.how_it_differs: Usually asymptomatic and found on routine prenatal screening; untreated infection is linked to preterm birth, low birth weight, and neonatal conjunctivitis or pneumonia, so screening at the first prenatal visit is standard.
Genital chlamydia in a prepubertal child raises concern for sexual abuse; infection can also present as neonatal conjunctivitis or afebrile pneumonia in infants born to infected mothers.
People with HIV or other immunosuppression may have more persistent or severe symptoms and higher rates of repeat infection, and co-infection with gonorrhea is more likely.
Less often considered, so diagnosis is delayed; presentation is the same but clinicians may attribute discharge or dysuria to urinary tract infection or atrophy instead.
missing_classic_features: Being in the usual screening age group

general.moderate: Mildly uncomfortable, may shift in the chair with pelvic or scrotal pain
general.severe: Ill-appearing, guarding the lower abdomen, reluctant to move

findings.maneuver: Insert a speculum and inspect the cervix
Move the cervix side to side with the examining fingers
Swab the cervix or observe after speculum insertion
Inspect the urethral meatus and strip the urethra

findings.finding: Tenderness and induration of the epididymis, usually unilateral
Relief of pain with elevation (suggests epididymitis rather than torsion)

findings.maneuver: Stroke the inner thigh and observe the scrotum
findings.finding: Cremasteric reflex present (argues against testicular torsion)

findings.maneuver: Assess for rebound tenderness or ask the patient to cough
Inspect the oral cavity and pharynx
Inspect the skin, including palms and soles

findings.finding: No joint swelling, warmth, or tenderness

labs.caveat: Sterile pyuria — leukocyte esterase may be positive while the urine culture is negative; this is a common clue to urethritis rather than a urinary tract infection.
White cells in urine without bacteriuria supports urethritis or cervicitis.
A positive nitrite points toward a true urinary tract infection rather than chlamydial urethritis.
Usually normal in uncomplicated urethritis or cervicitis; a rise suggests ascending infection such as pelvic inflammatory disease or epididymitis.
Nonspecific; may be mildly elevated with pelvic inflammatory disease.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or treatment; also rules out ectopic pregnancy when pelvic pain is present.

imaging.preferred_when: Pelvic pain, suspected pelvic inflammatory disease, or possible pregnancy

findings.text: Normal ovaries and tubes in uncomplicated cervicitis or urethritis
Thickened, fluid-filled fallopian tubes (pyosalpinx) with pelvic inflammatory disease

imaging.preferred_when: Testicular pain or swelling when torsion is a concern

findings.text: Enlarged, hyperemic epididymis with preserved or increased testicular flow (epididymitis)
Absent or reduced testicular flow (testicular torsion — a must-not-miss alternative)

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

findings.text: Usually normal; not needed for uncomplicated genital chlamydia
Tubal thickening, pelvic fluid, or tubo-ovarian abscess when infection has ascended

initial.why: Rules out pregnancy and ectopic pregnancy before imaging or antibiotics
Sterile pyuria supports urethritis and helps exclude a urinary tract infection
Looks for tubo-ovarian abscess or free fluid
initial.only_if: pelvic pain, adnexal tenderness, or suspected pelvic inflammatory disease

confirmatory.test: Nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) for Chlamydia trachomatis on first-catch urine
confirmatory.why: Preferred noninvasive test in males and in patients who decline a swab

confirmatory.test: Nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) for Chlamydia trachomatis on a vaginal or endocervical swab
confirmatory.why: Preferred specimen in females; self-collected vaginal swabs are acceptable

confirmatory.test: Nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) for Chlamydia trachomatis on a rectal swab
confirmatory.why: Detects rectal infection in patients reporting anal sex

confirmatory.test: Nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) for Chlamydia trachomatis on a pharyngeal swab
confirmatory.why: Detects pharyngeal infection in patients reporting oral sex

supporting.test: Nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) for Neisseria gonorrhoeae
supporting.why: Co-infection is common and changes treatment
Recommended for anyone diagnosed with an STI

supporting.test: Rapid plasma reagin (RPR) or treponemal test for syphilis
supporting.why: Recommended STI screening at the same visit

supporting.test: Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody
supporting.why: STI screening in patients with a new diagnosis
Evaluates concurrent bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis
Excludes a true urinary tract infection when pyuria is present
supporting.only_if: dysuria with positive leukocyte esterase or nitrite

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Rarely changes management of uncomplicated chlamydia; reserve for suspected abscess or an unclear surgical abdomen
Nonspecific and does not change management
Nonspecific and does not change management
No role unless the patient is dehydrated or systemically ill
No role in pelvic or scrotal pain from an STI

decision_points: Pregnancy test before imaging or antibiotics in anyone who could be pregnant
NAAT is the test of choice; culture is reserved for rare situations such as suspected treatment failure or medico-legal cases
Test all exposed sites (urine or vaginal/cervical, rectal, pharyngeal) based on reported sexual practices
Treat empirically for pelvic inflammatory disease when cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, or uterine tenderness is present, without waiting for NAAT results
Test and treat partners; patients should abstain from sex until 7 days after single-dose therapy or completion of a 7-day regimen and until partners are treated
Repeat testing about 3 months after treatment because reinfection is common
Sudden severe unilateral testicular pain with an absent cremasteric reflex is torsion until proven otherwise — do not wait for NAAT

differential.name: Gonorrhea
differential.why_considered: Nearly identical presentation with urethral or cervical discharge and dysuria; co-infection is common.
differential.trigger: Purulent, copious discharge or known partner with gonorrhea

history: More abrupt onset with heavier, thicker discharge
Higher likelihood of symptomatic presentation in men
exam: Profuse purulent urethral or cervical discharge
May have more marked pelvic tenderness if ascending
labs: Gram stain of urethral discharge showing gram-negative intracellular diplococci in men

differential.name: Trichomoniasis
differential.why_considered: Vaginal discharge and dysuria in a sexually active patient.

differential.name: Bacterial vaginosis
differential.why_considered: Vaginal discharge and odor without prominent dysuria.

history: Thin gray discharge with a fishy odor, worse after intercourse
exam: Homogeneous discharge coating the vaginal walls

differential.name: Herpes simplex genital infection
differential.why_considered: Genital pain, dysuria, and discharge in a sexually active patient.

history: Prodrome of tingling or burning before lesions
exam: Multiple painful vesicles or ulcers on the genitalia
labs: Positive HSV PCR from a lesion swab
Tzanck smear showing multinucleated giant cells

history: No new sexual partner or discharge
exam: Suprapubic tenderness without cervical motion tenderness
labs: Positive urine nitrite and leukocyte esterase

differential.name: Ectopic pregnancy
differential.why_considered: Lower abdominal or pelvic pain in a patient who could be pregnant.
differential.trigger: Any patient with pelvic pain who could be pregnant

imaging: No intrauterine pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound

differential.name: Testicular torsion
differential.trigger: Sudden severe unilateral testicular pain with nausea or vomiting

imaging: Absent or reduced testicular blood flow on Doppler ultrasound

differential.name: Reactive arthritis
differential.why_considered: Joint complaints in a patient with a recent STI.

history: Joint pain and swelling weeks after urethritis or cervicitis

severity.mild: Asymptomatic or minimal symptoms; detected on routine screening or partner notification; no systemic signs.
severity.moderate: Symptomatic urethritis or cervicitis with discharge, dysuria, or postcoital bleeding; no fever or peritoneal signs.
severity.severe: Ascending infection such as pelvic inflammatory disease or epididymitis with fever, pelvic or scrotal pain, and leukocytosis.
severity.critical: Ruptured tubo-ovarian abscess with generalized peritonitis and sepsis; hypotension, tachycardia, and diffuse abdominal rigidity.

red_flags.finding: Sudden severe unilateral testicular pain with absent cremasteric reflex
red_flags.meaning: Testicular torsion until proven otherwise; requires immediate urologic evaluation

red_flags.finding: Positive pregnancy test with pelvic pain or bleeding
Diffuse abdominal rigidity or rebound tenderness
red_flags.meaning: Peritonitis, possibly from a ruptured tubo-ovarian abscess
Sepsis; needs urgent resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics

red_flags.finding: High fever with severe pelvic pain
red_flags.meaning: Tubo-ovarian abscess or severe pelvic inflammatory disease

complications.name: Tubo-ovarian abscess
clues: Pelvic pain unresponsive to oral antibiotics

complications.name: Infertility
clues: History of recurrent or untreated chlamydia

complications.name: Ectopic pregnancy
clues: Missed period with pelvic pain and bleeding

complications.name: Neonatal conjunctivitis
clues: Eye discharge and redness in an infant born to an infected mother

complications.name: Neonatal pneumonia
clues: Afebrile pneumonia in an infant 2–12 weeks old

special_populations.differences: Usually asymptomatic and found on routine prenatal screening; untreated infection is linked to preterm birth, low birth weight, and neonatal conjunctivitis or pneumonia. Screening at the first prenatal visit is standard, and treatment with azithromycin or amoxicillin is recommended.
Genital chlamydia in a prepubertal child raises concern for sexual abuse; infection can also present as neonatal conjunctivitis or afebrile pneumonia in infants born to infected mothers.
People with HIV or other immunosuppression may have more persistent or severe symptoms and higher rates of repeat infection, and co-infection with gonorrhea is more likely.
Less often considered, so diagnosis is delayed; presentation is the same but clinicians may attribute discharge or dysuria to urinary tract infection or atrophy instead.

key_questions.question: Do you have any symptoms, or are you here because a partner tested positive or because of routine screening?
key_questions.looking_for: Many patients are asymptomatic; partner notification or screening is a common reason for presentation

key_questions.question: What symptoms have you noticed — discharge, burning with urination, pelvic or belly pain, bleeding between periods or after sex?
key_questions.looking_for: Thin discharge, dysuria, postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding, or pelvic pain

key_questions.question: When did your symptoms start?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset about 1–3 weeks after exposure; often present for weeks before care is sought

key_questions.question: Have you had a new sex partner or more than one partner in the past year?
key_questions.looking_for: New or multiple partners raises pretest probability and guides testing

key_questions.question: Do you use condoms? How consistently?
Do you have sex with men, women, or both? Do you have vaginal, anal, or oral sex?
key_questions.looking_for: Determines which sites to test — urine or vaginal/cervical, rectal, and pharyngeal

key_questions.question: Has a current or past partner been diagnosed with an STI, or had discharge or burning with urination?
key_questions.looking_for: Partner with a known STI or urethral symptoms strongly supports the diagnosis

key_questions.question: Have you ever had an STI before, including chlamydia or gonorrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior STI increases risk of reinfection and complications

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your first day of your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy changes treatment choices and, with pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy must be excluded

key_questions.question: Do you have any lower belly pain, pain with sex, or fever?
key_questions.looking_for: Suggests ascending infection such as pelvic inflammatory disease

key_questions.question: Any pain or swelling in one testicle?
key_questions.looking_for: Epididymitis; sudden severe pain suggests torsion instead

key_questions.question: Any rectal pain, discharge, or bleeding? Any sore throat?
key_questions.looking_for: Rectal or pharyngeal infection based on exposure

key_questions.question: Any joint pain or swelling, eye redness, or rash?
key_questions.looking_for: Reactive arthritis or another STI such as secondary syphilis

key_questions.question: Are you taking any antibiotics or other medications right now?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent antibiotics may affect test results; drug interactions matter for treatment choice

key_questions.question: Do you have any medication allergies, especially to antibiotics?
key_questions.looking_for: Penicillin or cephalosporin allergy changes the regimen

key_questions.question: Do you have any concerns about safety at home, or has anyone pressured you into sex?
key_questions.looking_for: Intimate partner violence or coercion, which changes counseling and follow-up

reasoning_points: Sexual history identifies a new or multiple partners, inconsistent condom use, or a partner with a known STI
Symptoms of urethritis or cervicitis — discharge, dysuria, postcoital bleeding — or the patient may be entirely asymptomatic
Onset about 1–3 weeks after exposure fits the incubation period
Exam may show mucopurulent cervical discharge, a friable cervix, or urethral discharge; cervical motion tenderness suggests pelvic inflammatory disease
Sterile pyuria on urinalysis supports urethritis rather than a urinary tract infection
Nucleic acid amplification testing of the appropriate sites confirms the diagnosis
Gonorrhea co-infection, HIV, and syphilis should be tested at the same visit
Pregnancy must be excluded before treatment and because of the risk of ectopic pregnancy with pelvic pain
Partners must be treated and the patient should abstain from sex until therapy is completed

easy: Sexually active young adult with a new partner and no symptoms, presenting after a partner tested positive
Thin urethral discharge with dysuria in a young man
Mucopurulent cervical discharge with postcoital bleeding in a young woman
medium: Asymptomatic patient detected on routine screening with no complaints at all
Dysuria with sterile pyuria and a negative urine culture
Rectal infection presenting with rectal pain or discharge
Patient with concurrent gonorrhea and chlamydia
hard: Pelvic inflammatory disease with fever and cervical motion tenderness where chlamydia is the underlying cause
Epididymitis with unilateral testicular pain where torsion must first be excluded
Pregnant patient found on routine prenatal screening with no symptoms
Older adult whose discharge or dysuria is mistakenly attributed to urinary tract infection or atrophy
Prepubertal child with genital chlamydia raising concern for sexual abuse
